blocks.x: Mike Ditka, the ferocious titan who defined the scrappy determination of the Chicago Bears as player and coach, and the football commentator and product endorser whose sharpness and good humor made Sunday afternoons feel like quality time with dad, has died at 86. An announcement was posted on X by WSCR’s Jarrett Payton on Friday, who shared a statement on behalf of the Ditka family.

“It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, grandfather, and friend, Mike Ditka,” the post read. “While the world knew Mike as a Hall of Fame football player, legendary coach, and leader of the Chicago Bears’ Super Bowl XX championship team, we knew him as the heart of our family. Mike will be missed beyond measure and remembered forever.”

Indeed, the world’s image of Mike Ditka as a dominant presence in the National Football League, with his push-broom mustache and wry, crinkled grin that belied a gruffness that rankled many who worked with him, is just shorthand for a life defined by as many setbacks as triumphs. Michael Keller Ditka’s storied career took shape during high school in the steel town of Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, where he was encouraged to play for the Pitt Panthers at the University Of Pittsburgh. Before he could pursue his ambition of becoming a dentist, Ditka led the Panthers for three successful seasons. Despite this versatility on the gridiron, football wasn’t Ditka’s only college interest. His bullish frame, which he would use to his constant advantage during play, established him as a three-sport varsity athlete in football, basketball, and baseball, and an intramural wrestling champion for his school.

Ditka’s belligerent prowess as a quadruple-threat was well-known: Kentucky basketball coach Adolph Rupp once referred to him as a “hatchet man” on the court, while the Panthers’ wrestling coach, Rex Peery, once said Ditka had the grit to be an NCAA wrestling champion if he’d gone for varsity. This scrappiness benefitted Ditka all his life. By the time he signed with the Chicago Bears in 1961 (as a first-round draft pick), his reputation as a heavy-hitter preceded him. He was known for his brute strength and brick-wall blocks, and a noted impatience for fellow players he felt weren’t hitting hard enough during practice. These qualities made him an asset on the field and a source of aggravation for the Bears’ owner, George Halas, who ultimately traded Ditka to the Philadelphia Eagles in April 1967 in a fit of exhaustion. “Mr. Halas made the right decision,” Ditka recalled in 2013. “I was a pain in the ass.”

Ditka considered his time away from the Bears a personal low, and took to drink during his short-lived Eagles run. “I really drank a lot,” he said in Ditka: An Autobiography, which he co-wrote with the Chicago Tribune‘s Don Pierson. “Almost killed myself drinking.” Yet, like most everything in Ditka’s life, he endured this low point with the Eagles, and that perseverance eventually led to Dallas Cowboys coach Tom Landry tossing him a career lifeline in 1969. Under Landry’s mentorship, Ditka renewed his focus, playing for the team until 1972. After he and his team defeated the Miami Dolphins in Super Bowl VI, he accepted an assistant coach role from Landry from 1973 to 1981. “[Before the Cowboys,] I was done, finished, and I had made the decision to retire,” he said during a jersey-retiring ceremony in 2013. “I was hurt all the time; I didn’t enjoy the game. I was in bad shape physically, mentally, and socially… I only came back because of a call from Tom, who told me he was willing to take a chance on me, if I was willing to take a chance on myself.”

As his reputation grew on the sidelines, where Ditka could be seen bellowing at players next to the comparatively stoic Landry, a call from Chicago would steer Ditka back to the city that he would ultimately call his home. George Halas, now in his eighties, had chosen Ditka over a heavy field of candidates—a move precipitated by a letter Ditka sent to the Bears owner in 1981, which he hoped would mend their professional and personal rifts and put him in contention as the Bears’ head coach someday. The letter seemed to have worked. “I asked [Tom], ‘Do you think I’m ready?’ and he said, ‘Yes, I think you’re ready.’ An endorsement like that from Coach Landry was all I needed,” Ditka said.

And so, from 1982 to 1992, Mike Ditka coached the Chicago Bears. His biggest achievement, arguably, and one that remains among the most defining moments for the team, was leading the Bears to the franchise’s first and, to date, only Super Bowl title in 1985. This moment of glory eclipsed an earlier DUI arrest that year, and came two years after Halas’ death on Halloween 1983, a feat Halas had not himself accomplished despite serving as the Bears’ coach across 40 seasons. Ditka was also inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1988, the first tight end to ever receive the honor.

Yet Ditka’s time as head coach following this victory was not without incident. His long-standing rivalry with Buddy Ryan, the Bears’ defensive coordinator from 1978 until just after the Bears’ ’85 Super Bowl win, added friction to Ditka’s already contentious tenure. (The Chicago Tribune reported Ditka saying upon Ryan’s exit, “I’m not happy he’s gone—I’m elated” and that “Never again in history will an assistant coach get as much credit as Buddy did.”) After a disappointing 5–11 season, Ditka was fired as the Bears’ head coach in 1993. He’d spend the next four years as an analyst and color commentator for NBC, and appeared twice on Saturday Night Live to poke fun at his persona as “Da Coach” during the show’s famous skit, “Bill Swerski’s Superfans.”

His subsequent three-season stint as head coach for the New Orleans Saints from 1997 to 1999 resumed Ditka’s testy relationship with quarterbacks, leading to a disastrous cycle through seven QBs. This period saw the outsized Ditka personality truly come to the fore. When the Saints signed Ricky Williams in 1999 (a controversial move on its own, having cost the Saints their 1999 and 2000 draft picks), he interviewed alongside his new running back wearing a wig of ridiculous dreadlocks; when the duo appeared on the August 1999 cover of ESPN Magazine, Ditka wore a tuxedo next to Williams in a wedding dress, with the headline “For Better Or Worse.” After a grueling 3–13 season in 1999, the Saints and Ditka parted ways.

Yet he was never far from fame. Endorsements that came his way as far back as 1985 led to semi-regular appearances on television in commercials for Budweiser, McDonald’s, and Campbell’s soups. In the 1990s, he boosted Circuit City and Hanes (“Even us tough guys need comfort underneath!”), and perhaps most infamously, he appeared in a line of commercials endorsing the erectile dysfunction medication Levitra. “Do what I did, and ask your doctor about Levitra!” he said, tossing around a football.

The Ditka brand extended to merchandise in the vein of other former athlete-turned-media personalities, like George Foreman and Bo Jackson. Soon, Ditka-brand mustards and sauces were available to buy in stores, like Ditka’s Real Steak Sauce and Ditka’s Chicago Style Italian Beef & Gravy. And no piece on Mike Ditka would be complete without a mention of his restaurant endeavors. Ditka’s, his first restaurant, opened in October 1986 on Ontario Street in Chicago and eventually grew into a regional chain of steakhouses.
He is survived by his wife, Diana, and his four children with his first wife, Marge Dougherty.
